title: Game of the Century
subtitle: Byrne vs Fischer, 1956 — a 13-year-old sacrifices his queen.
goals: Play Fischer's Na4!! and Be6!! yourself
Trade a queen for a coordinated army

steps.say: New York, 1956. Donald Byrne, one of America's strongest masters, is playing a 13-year-old named Bobby Fischer — and has just played 11.Bg5?, one careless tempo. What follows was christened 'The Game of the Century' before the year was out. Fischer's response begins a combination that runs TWENTY moves deep and includes the most celebrated queen sacrifice in modern chess. You're Bobby. Find move one.

steps.prompt: White's queen sits on c5, his king still on e1. Fischer's 11th move looks like it hangs a knight — play it, and the follow-up that shows why it doesn't!
hints: Na4!! offers the knight to deflect White's c3 knight away from e4 — if Nxa4, then Nxe4! and White's position collapses on the loose e4/g5 squares.
Play Na4, and after Qa3 Nxc3 bxc3, take the e4 pawn — the g5 bishop now hangs to tricks and White's king is stuck forever.

line.say: The move that announced Fischer to the world. The knight is 'hanging' — but Nxa4 loses to Nxe4!, when both g5 and c5 fall apart...
Byrne declined, so the knight takes anyway — deflecting the b-pawn...

The point: a clean central pawn, tempo against the g5 bishop, and White's king will NEVER castle. A 13-year-old just out-calculated a master in his own position — and the real fireworks haven't even started.

rejections.say: Passive — and White consolidates with Bh6 or e5, a happy man. Fischer's judgment: when the enemy king lingers in the center, INVEST material to keep it there. Na4!!
Right idea, wrong order! Nxe4 Nxe4 and the knight on b6 never joined — the deflection Na4!! comes first, so that the recapture on c3/e4 arrives with the whole army.

steps.wrongSay: The knight move looks like a blunder — that's exactly why it's immortal. Aim at White's overloaded c3 knight.
steps.successSay: Na4!! — judged by many the finest single move of the 1950s. Played by a child, now replayed by you.

steps.prompt: Six moves later: Byrne just played Bc5 hitting your queen, certain he's finally winning material. Fischer's reply is THE move of the century. Your queen stays en prise — find it!
hints: Don't move the queen — improve the piece that unleashes everything. A quiet bishop move leaves your queen hanging AND wins by force.
Be6!! If Bxb6, then Bxc4+ begins a windmill of knight checks that harvests White's whole queenside — a queen traded for an army.

line.say: THE MOVE OF THE CENTURY. The queen hangs; Fischer doesn't care. Declining with Bxe6 loses to Qb5+! forking, so Byrne must take the queen — and feed the windmill you'll play next. A 13-year-old, offering his queen to a master, correct in every line: this is why the game has its name.

rejections.say: dxc5! — wait: the d4 pawn recaptures and White is FINE, material even, attack gone. The century move keeps the queen en prise: Be6!!, because the windmill it unleashes is worth more than she is.
The queen scurries to safety — and Qxa5 wait, no: simply, White trades queens and survives. Fischer's Be6!! refuses the whole question: the bishop check on c4 is worth more than the queen.

steps.wrongSay: Every queen retreat lets White breathe. The winning move doesn't touch the queen at all.
steps.successSay: Be6!! — chess's most famous quiet move. Now collect the payment.

steps.prompt: Byrne took the queen. Now the harvest: eleven moves of checks — bishop, then the knight windmill — ending with your material restored WITH interest. Play it all!
hints: Bxc4+ first, then the knight dances: Ne2+, Nxd4+, Ne2+, Nc3+ — every hop a check, every other hop a capture — then finally take the b6 bishop back.
The full sequence: Bxc4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nxd4+ Kg1 Ne2+ Kf1 Nc3+ Kg1 axb6.

line.say: First blood — the bishop that made Be6!! possible collects a bishop...
...swing and CAPTURE — the d4 pawn falls with another check...
...and out with a third check, hitting the d1 rook on the way...

Harvest complete: the a-pawn quietly collects the b6 bishop. Count Fischer's haul for the queen: rook, TWO bishops and a pawn — plus a raging attack. Byrne played on to move 41 and was mated by a 13-year-old. The Game of the Century, and you just played its heart.

rejections.say: Greed before checks! Qxc3 — White's queen kills your windmill conductor and survives. The checks come FIRST — Bxc4+! — so White's queen never gets a move.

steps.wrongSay: Eleven forced moves, every Black move a check until the last. The light bishop leads.
steps.successSay: Queen for rook, two bishops and a pawn — arithmetic even a master couldn't accept until it was on the board. Immortality, re-enacted.
